proofs.proof_tex:
Write
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}
 =\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}^{\partial}
   (d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa).
\]
The hypotheses that \(m\) is odd, every arrow \(j\to i\) of \(G\) has \(j<i\), and \(u\to v\in G\) are explicit.  Hence \(\mathrm{lem{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}class\mbox{-}nonempty}\), together with
\[
 \kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1},
\]
gives \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\ne\varnothing\).  Thus the uniform assertion below is over a nonempty class.  Fix \(d,m,G,\mathcal Z,\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa\), with \(\mathcal Z\) finite and nonempty, let \(n\to\infty\), and take all suprema below over \(P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\).

The fine-parameter set underlying \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\) is compact.  Indeed, the graph zero restrictions, the bounds \(|A_{ij}|\le L\), \(|A_{ii}|\le1-\gamma\), \(d_{\min}I_d\preceq D\preceq d_{\max}I_d\), and the two inequalities
\[
 \min_{j\to i\in G}|C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\ge\kappa,
 \qquad
 \min_{i\in V}m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\ge\kappa
\]
are closed conditions, and the entry and innovation bounds make the parameter set bounded.  The lower innovation bound makes every \(D\) positive definite.  Since \(A\) is lower triangular, its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, so \(\rho(A)\le1-\gamma<1\).  Each \((A,D)\) therefore determines a unique stationary Gaussian law.

Put
\[
 \vartheta=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(M_0,M_1),
 \qquad
 \widehat\vartheta=\operatorname{vec}_{s}(\widehat M_0,\widehat M_1),
 \qquad
 \rho=1-\gamma.
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}coarse\mbox{-}law\mbox{-}reduction}\),
\[
 Y_s=BY_{s-1}+\eta_s,
 \qquad B=A^m,
 \qquad
 \eta_s\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}
 \sigma(Y_{s-1},Y_{s-2},\ldots),
 \qquad \eta_s\sim N(0,Q),
\]
and
\[
 B=M_1M_0^{-1},
 \qquad Q=M_0-BM_0B^\top.
\]
The innovation bounds in \(\mathrm{def{:}regular\mbox{-}class}\) imply
\[
 Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top\succeq D\succeq d_{\min}I_d.
\]
Stationarity consequently gives
\[
 M_0=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^kQ(B^k)^\top
     =\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}A^rD(A^r)^\top
     \succeq Q\succeq d_{\min}I_d.                       \tag{1}
\]
There is also a uniform upper bound.  Lower triangularity, the entry envelope, and \(|A_{ii}|\le\rho<1\) imply, by expansion along nondecreasing vertex walks, that a finite \(C_A=C_A(d,L,\rho)\) satisfies
\[
 \lVert A^r\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le C_A(r+1)^{d-1}\rho^{(r-d+1)_+},
 \qquad r\ge0.                                             \tag{2}
\]
There are at most \(d-1\) strict increases in a walk; choosing their locations gives the polynomial factor in \((2)\), and all remaining steps are diagonal and contribute at most \(\rho\).  Therefore
\[
 M_0\preceq
 d_{\max}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\lVert A^r\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^2 I_d
 \preceq C_0I_d                                             \tag{3}
\]
for a finite \(C_0=C_0(d,L,\gamma,d_{\max})\).  Equations \((1)\) and \((3)\) make inversion of \(M_0\) uniformly legitimate.  Thus
\[
 (M_0,M_1)\longmapsto(B,Q)
 =\bigl(M_1M_0^{-1},\ M_0-M_1M_0^{-1}M_1^\top\bigr)         \tag{4}
\]
is twice continuously differentiable, with uniformly bounded first and second derivatives, on a common neighborhood of the population moment set.

We next analyze the graph-recursive inverse.  Since \(B_{ii}=A_{ii}^m\), derivative separation gives
\[
 \left|\frac{\partial B_{ii}}{\partial A_{ii}}\right|
 =m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\ge\kappa.                                \tag{5}
\]
Oddness of \(m\) makes the real diagonal root unique.  Its first derivative is \((mA_{ii}^{m-1})^{-1}\), and its second derivative is
\[
 -\frac{m-1}{m^2A_{ii}^{2m-1}}.
\]
The second derivative is uniformly bounded because \((5)\) implies \(|A_{ii}|\ge(\kappa/m)^{1/(m-1)}>0\).  For every allowed off-diagonal coordinate, membership in \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\) gives
\[
 |C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\ge\kappa.                            \tag{6}
\]
The recursion proved in \(\mathrm{thm{:}odd\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}identification}\) is
\[
 A_{ij}=\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})}.       \tag{7}
\]
At endpoint gap \(i-j\), the polynomial \(R_{ij,m}\) contains only coordinates recovered at smaller endpoint gaps.  Starting with the diagonal roots and inducting over the finitely many gaps, \((6)\)--\((7)\) express every recovered coordinate as a twice continuously differentiable function of \(B\).  Compactness and continuity give a common neighborhood on which the absolute values in \((5)\) and \((6)\) are at least \(\kappa/2\); on it, the first and second derivatives of the full recursion are uniformly bounded.  The innovation recursion is also smooth because each of its denominators satisfies
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}\ge1,                           \tag{8}
\]
although the queried transfer itself depends only on \(A\).

For \(z\in\mathcal Z\subset\mathbb T\),
\[
 |1-A_{vv}z|\ge1-|A_{vv}|\ge\gamma.                         \tag{9}
\]
The coefficient-to-transfer map is therefore twice continuously differentiable on the same common neighborhood.  Direct differentiation yields
\[
 \mathrm dh_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{z}{1-A_{vv}z}\,\mathrm dA_{vu}
  +\frac{A_{vu}z^2}{(1-A_{vv}z)^2}\,\mathrm dA_{vv}.        \tag{10}
\]
Let \(F(\vartheta)\) stack the real and imaginary parts of \((h_{uv}(z))_{z\in\mathcal Z}\), and let \(J_h(\vartheta)\) be the Jacobian of the composite of \((4)\), the graph recursion, and \((10)\).  The uniform second-derivative bounds give, on the common neighborhood,
\[
 F(\widehat\vartheta)-F(\vartheta)
 =J_h(\vartheta)(\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)+r_n,
 \qquad
 \lVert r_n\rVert
 \le C\lVert\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta\rVert^2.           \tag{11}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}uniform\mbox{-}gaussian\mbox{-}lag\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}clt}\), \(\sqrt n(\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)\) is uniformly tight and
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\vartheta-\vartheta)
 \Longrightarrow N(0,\Omega(P))                              \tag{12}
\]
uniformly in \(P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\).  Uniform tightness makes the neighborhood event in \((11)\) have probability tending to one uniformly and gives, for every \(\epsilon>0\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 P\!\left(\sqrt n\lVert r_n\rVert>\epsilon\right)
 \longrightarrow0.                                           \tag{13}
\]
Combining \((11)\)--\((13)\) proves
\[
 \sqrt n\{F(\widehat\vartheta)-F(\vartheta)\}
 \Longrightarrow N(0,\Sigma_h(P)),
 \qquad
 \Sigma_h(P)=J_h(\vartheta)\Omega(P)J_h(\vartheta)^\top      \tag{14}
\]
uniformly over the class.

The covariance series in the lag-moment central limit lemma converges absolutely and uniformly, and each summand is a continuous Gaussian Isserlis polynomial in the coarse covariance sequence.  Thus \(P\mapsto\Omega(P)\), and hence \(P\mapsto\Sigma_h(P)\), is continuous.  Let \(\widetilde\Omega\) be the Isserlis plug-in estimator supplied by that lemma, let \(\widehat\Omega\) be its projection onto the positive-semidefinite cone, and compute \(\widehat J_h\) by the same recursion at the empirical moments.  Since the eigenvalues of \(B=A^m\) have modulus at most \((1-\gamma)^m<1\), uniform consistency of \(\widehat B\) and continuity of spectral radius imply
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 P(\widehat B\text{ is not stable})\longrightarrow0.
\]
The central limit lemma gives \(\widehat\Omega-\Omega(P)=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly; projection onto the positive-semidefinite cone cannot increase Frobenius distance to the positive-semidefinite target.  The smoothness established above also gives \(\widehat J_h-J_h=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\) uniformly.  Consequently
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_h
 =\widehat J_h\widehat\Omega\widehat J_h^\top
 =\Sigma_h(P)+o_{\mathbb P}(1)                              \tag{15}
\]
uniformly, and \(\widehat\Sigma_h\) is positive semidefinite.

It remains to control rank changes in the Gaussian critical value.  Define
\[
 \widetilde M_0=n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}Y_{s-1}Y_{s-1}^\top.
\]
The empirical-moment definition gives the exact boundary identity
\[
 \widehat M_0-\widetilde M_0
 =n^{-1}(Y_nY_n^\top-Y_0Y_0^\top).                         \tag{16}
\]
The uniform covariance bound \((3)\) makes the right-hand side of \((16)\) equal to \(o_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\) uniformly.  From the coarse innovation equation,
\[
 \widehat M_1
 =B\widetilde M_0+n^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\eta_sY_{s-1}^\top.
\]
Using \((1)\), \((16)\), and a first-order inverse expansion therefore yields
\[
 \sqrt n\,\operatorname{vec}(\widehat B-B)
 =\operatorname{vec}\!\left(
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\eta_sY_{s-1}^\top M_0^{-1}
 \right)+o_{\mathbb P}(1).                                  \tag{17}
\]
The summands are martingale differences.  Independence of \(\eta_s\) from the past gives their covariance, up to the fixed vectorization convention, as
\[
 \Gamma_B=M_0^{-1}\otimes Q.
\]
By \((1)\), \((3)\), and \(Q\succeq d_{\min}I_d\),
\[
 \Gamma_B\succeq c_BI_{d^2},
 \qquad c_B=\frac{d_{\min}}{C_0}>0.                         \tag{18}
\]

Because \(u\to v\in G\), equation \((7)\) recovers \(A_{vu}\) as an allowed coordinate, while its remainder uses only smaller gaps.  Hence
\[
 \frac{\partial A_{vu}}{\partial B_{vu}}
 =\frac{1}{C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})},
 \qquad
 \frac{\partial A_{vv}}{\partial B_{vu}}=0.                 \tag{19}
\]
Furthermore, \(|A_{ii}|\le\rho<1\) gives
\[
 |C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})|
 \le\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}|A_{vv}|^r|A_{uu}|^{m-1-r}
 \le m,
 \qquad
 |1-A_{vv}z|\le1+|A_{vv}|\le2.                              \tag{20}
\]
Combining \((10)\), \((19)\), and \((20)\),
\[
 \left|\frac{\partial h_{uv}(z)}{\partial B_{vu}}\right|
 =\frac{1}{|C_m(A_{vv},A_{uu})|\,|1-A_{vv}z|}
 \ge\frac{1}{2m}.                                           \tag{21}
\]
Equations \((18)\)--\((21)\) imply that the limiting complex coordinate \(Z_h(z)\) satisfies
\[
 \mathbb E|Z_h(z)|^2\ge\frac{c_B}{4m^2}>0                  \tag{22}
\]
uniformly for every \(z\in\mathcal Z\).  Thus the limiting vector is never identically zero, although its covariance can be singular because coordinates at distinct frequencies may be linearly dependent.

For a real vector written in complex-coordinate pairs, define
\[
 \lVert x\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}
 =\max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt{x_{\Re,z}^2+x_{\Im,z}^2}.
\]
For \(\Sigma\succeq0\), let \(Z_\Sigma\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) and define
\[
 c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma)
 =\inf\bigl\{t:
 \Pr(\lVert Z_\Sigma\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}\le t)
 \ge1-\alpha\bigr\}.                                      \tag{23}
\]
The parameter set is compact, \(\Sigma_h(P)\) is continuous, and \((22)\) keeps its range away from the zero matrix.  On the support subspace of any nonzero centered Gaussian vector, its law has a positive density and the restriction of \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathcal Z,\infty}\) is a norm.  Each norm sphere has Lebesgue measure zero in that subspace and each nonempty norm annulus has positive measure.  The distribution function in \((23)\) is therefore continuous and strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\), with no atom at zero.  If \(\Sigma_j\to\Sigma\), continuity of the positive-semidefinite square root gives \(Z_{\Sigma_j}\Rightarrow Z_\Sigma\); strict continuity of the limiting distribution then gives
\[
 c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_j)\longrightarrow c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma).
\]
Thus the quantile map is continuous on the compact covariance range.  Equation \((15)\) implies
\[
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}
 =c_{1-\alpha}(\widehat\Sigma_h)
 =c_{1-\alpha}(\Sigma_h(P))+o_{\mathbb P}(1)                \tag{24}
\]
uniformly.

If uniform coverage failed, there would be a sequence \(P_n\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\) along which the coverage error stayed bounded away from zero.  Compactness supplies a subsequence for which the fine parameters, and hence \(\Sigma_h(P_n)\), converge.  The uniform limit \((14)\), the critical-value convergence \((24)\), and the absence of probability on the limiting boundary imply along that subsequence
\[
 \Pr_{P_n}\!\left(
 \max_{z\in\mathcal Z}\sqrt n\,
 |\widehat h_{uv}(z)-h_{uv}(z)|
 \le\widehat c_{1-\alpha}
 \right)\longrightarrow1-\alpha,                             \tag{25}
\]
which is a contradiction.  The event in \((25)\) is precisely
\[
 h_{uv}(z)\in
 \left\{w\in\mathbb C:
 |w-\widehat h_{uv}(z)|\le
 \frac{\widehat c_{1-\alpha}}{\sqrt n}
 \right\}
 \quad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z.
\]
This proves the stated uniform simultaneous Wald coverage, including when \(A_{vu}=0\) and when the limiting covariance is rank deficient across frequencies.

to the long-run Gaussian lag-moment covariance.  \sup_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}^{\partial}}

proposed_statement_changes.reason: The current claim describes the derivative restriction only ad hoc and permits a vacuous uniform assertion when the restricted family is empty. The replacement names the already defined derivative-separated class directly and adds the explicit oddness, labeled-order, queried-edge, and \(\kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}\) conditions that certify nonemptiness.

proposed.justification: The explicitly defined derivative-separated odd stratum is feasible exactly when \(\kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}\), and on that nonempty stratum it supports simultaneous uncertainty quantification without global branch inversion.
proposed.gap: Fine-grid process-graph Wald theory does not establish the uniform Jacobian and Taylor bounds created by an aliased triangular root recursion, nor the quantile argument needed when the cross-frequency Gaussian covariance changes rank.
proposed.consumer: Researchers can verify feasibility and the two separation margins directly, use simultaneous Wald disks when they hold, and revert to the exact branch-free inverse confidence set otherwise.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The replacement makes the proof spine explicit by adding the supplied labeled order and odd-factor assumptions used in the nonemptiness and inverse-recursion steps, while retaining the defined regular-class dependency used for compactness and moment bounds.

prose_updates.tldr: Subsampling turns a fine-grid process DAG into a matrix-root problem, so causal identification depends on the complete root-and-innovation fiber rather than on a selected numerical root. The paper gives parity-sharp graph recursion and exact transfer-aware algebraic certification. On the explicitly defined derivative-separated odd stratum, which is nonempty in the stated feasible separation range, a uniformly valid delta method yields simultaneous Wald disks. Globally, a finite-sample coarse-moment region is inverted through every branch, and the measurable constant-envelope fallback reproduces the deterministic moment box pathwise, preserving coverage without claiming a strict adaptive gain.

project_justification.fill: The project gives a parity-sharp graph recursion, a universal even-factor same-law obstruction, a total transfer-aware CAD fallback with exact witnesses, simultaneous Wald disks on an explicit nonempty derivative-separated odd class under \(\kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}\), and finite-sample branch-free inversion of a rationally rounded coarse-moment region. The covariance-envelope fallback is measurable and pathwise no wider because it exactly reproduces the deterministic box; it is a validity fallback, not an adaptive improvement.

sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Estimate \((M_0,M_1)\) by overlapping empirical lag moments. When \(m\) is odd, the supplied order and queried edge hold, \(\kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}\), and the derivative-separated regular conditions hold, map the moments through \((\widehat B,\widehat Q)\), the graph recursion, and the rational transfer, and use the Isserlis long-run covariance with the recursive Jacobian for simultaneous Wald disks. Globally, invert the rationally outward-rounded moment box through all fine-grid branches; the constant covariance-envelope fallback is measurable and coincides pathwise with that deterministic box.

prose_updates.honest_scope: The algebraic identification and ambiguity results concern stable, ordered, finite-dimensional Gaussian VAR(1) systems with known subsampling factor, supplied labeled process DAG, and diagonal fine-grid innovation covariance. Under the explicit odd-factor, supplied-order, and queried-edge conditions, the Wald theorem applies to the derivative-separated regular class and asserts nonemptiness only when \(\kappa\le m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}\). The limiting covariance may be singular across frequencies but is uniformly nonzero in the queried-edge direction. Outside that class, inference uses branch-free inversion rather than branch selection. The constant covariance-envelope construction proves finite-sample validity and equality of widths with the deterministic box, not strict adaptive improvement. Exact CAD certifies termination rather than polynomial-time scalability, and executable witnesses require effective real-closed-field input. No claim is made about unknown causal order, unknown sampling factor, high-dimensional rates, VARMA or unit-root extensions, or the scientific validity of the Temperature--Ozone ordering.
